facts.one_liner: More than 2,000 natural sandstone arches in the red-rock desert outside Moab.
facts.why_go: Arches holds the world’s densest concentration of natural stone arches—over 2,000 of them—carved from salmon-coloured Entrada sandstone. Delicate Arch, the free-standing icon on Utah’s licence plates, is reached by a 3-mile round-trip hike across open slickrock, while the Windows Section and Devils Garden put dozens more arches within easy walking distance. Sunset sets the fins and spires glowing.
facts.best_time: March–May and September–October for comfortable hiking; summer is very hot, so hike at dawn or dusk.
facts.how_to_get_there: The entrance is about 5 miles north of Moab on US 191. The nearest airports are Canyonlands Regional (CNY) near Moab and Grand Junction, Colorado (about 2 hours).
facts.good_to_know: A timed-entry reservation has been required in peak season in recent years—check nps.gov before you go. Carry plenty of water; there is little shade.

facts.one_liner: A natural amphitheatre packed with thousands of orange-and-white hoodoos.
facts.why_go: Bryce Canyon is not one canyon but a series of natural amphitheatres eroded into the edge of the Paunsaugunt Plateau. The Bryce Amphitheater is filled with hoodoos—tall, thin spires of rock—that glow orange at sunrise. Rim viewpoints such as Sunrise, Sunset, Inspiration and Bryce Point are short walks from the road, and the Navajo Loop and Queen’s Garden trails drop you right among the spires. At over 8,000 feet, it is also a celebrated dark-sky park.
facts.best_time: May–October for hiking; winter brings snow-dusted hoodoos and quiet trails.
facts.how_to_get_there: About 4 hours’ drive from Las Vegas or Salt Lake City; the park road runs south from Utah Route 63 near Bryce Canyon City. A free seasonal shuttle serves the main viewpoints.
facts.good_to_know: The high elevation means cold nights even in summer, and the trails below the rim are steep on the climb back up.

facts.one_liner: Mist-wrapped ridges, wildflower meadows and historic log cabins in the southern Appalachians.
facts.why_go: Straddling the Tennessee–North Carolina border, Great Smoky Mountains is America’s most visited national park and a UNESCO World Heritage Site famed for its biodiversity. The blue haze that gives the range its name hangs over ancient forested ridges, while Cades Cove preserves log cabins, churches and open meadows where deer and black bears roam. Clingmans Dome and Newfound Gap give sweeping views, and hundreds of miles of trail include a stretch of the Appalachian Trail.
facts.best_time: April–May for wildflowers; mid-October for blazing autumn colour.
facts.how_to_get_there: Gateway towns are Gatlinburg, Tennessee, and Cherokee, North Carolina. Knoxville’s McGhee Tyson Airport (TYS) is about an hour from the Sugarlands Visitor Center.
facts.good_to_know: Entry is free, but a parking tag is required for vehicles parked more than 15 minutes. Cades Cove Loop Road is closed to cars on some mornings for cyclists—check the NPS schedule.

facts.one_liner: Granite peaks, rocky shores and glassy ponds on Maine’s Mount Desert Island.
facts.why_go: Acadia protects much of Mount Desert Island on the Maine coast, where pink granite mountains meet the cold Atlantic. Cadillac Mountain is the highest point on the US Atlantic seaboard, and from autumn to spring it is among the first places in the country to see the sunrise. The Park Loop Road links Sand Beach, Thunder Hole and Jordan Pond, while 45 miles of historic carriage roads are perfect for cycling and walking.
facts.best_time: June–October; late September to mid-October for autumn foliage.
facts.how_to_get_there: Bar Harbor is the gateway town. Fly to Bangor (BGR), about an hour away, or the small Hancock County–Bar Harbor airport; the free seasonal Island Explorer bus links Bar Harbor with park trailheads.
facts.good_to_know: A vehicle reservation is required for the Cadillac Summit Road in peak season. Parking at popular spots fills quickly—use the Island Explorer.

facts.one_liner: High alpine tundra, elk-filled meadows and 14,000-foot peaks along Trail Ridge Road.
facts.why_go: Rocky Mountain National Park straddles the Continental Divide in northern Colorado. Trail Ridge Road, the highest continuous paved road in the US, crosses miles of alpine tundra above 11,000 feet, while valleys such as Moraine Park fill with grazing elk—especially during the dramatic autumn rut. Longs Peak towers above more than 300 miles of trails leading to alpine lakes such as Bear Lake and Dream Lake.
facts.best_time: June–September when Trail Ridge Road is open; September–October for the elk rut and golden aspens.
facts.how_to_get_there: Estes Park, the main gateway, is about 1.5–2 hours’ drive from Denver International Airport (DEN).
facts.good_to_know: Timed-entry permits have been required in summer and early autumn—check NPS. Weather changes fast at altitude; afternoon thunderstorms are common.

facts.one_liner: Wild Pacific beaches, temperate rainforest and glacier-capped peaks in one park.
facts.why_go: Olympic National Park protects three distinct ecosystems on Washington’s Olympic Peninsula: more than 70 miles of rugged Pacific coastline with sea stacks and tide pools, the moss-draped Hoh and Quinault temperate rainforests, and the glaciated Olympic Mountains crowned by Mount Olympus. Hurricane Ridge offers easy alpine views, and Rialto, Ruby and Second beaches are known for their dramatic sea stacks at sunset. It is both a UNESCO World Heritage Site and a Biosphere Reserve.
facts.best_time: July–September for drier weather and open mountain roads; winter brings storm-watching on the coast.
facts.how_to_get_there: Port Angeles is the main gateway, about 2.5–3 hours from Seattle via ferry or road. There is no road through the park’s interior, so plan a loop on US 101.
facts.good_to_know: Check tide tables before beach hikes—some headlands can only be passed at low tide.

facts.one_liner: Jagged granite peaks rising straight out of the sagebrush flats of Jackson Hole.

Jenny Lake, String Lake and Jackson Lake mirror the peaks, Schwabacher Landing and Oxbow Bend are famous at sunrise, and moose, elk and bison graze the flats. facts.one_liner: Six million acres of wild tundra beneath North America’s tallest peak.
facts.why_go: Denali National Park and Preserve covers six million acres of Alaskan wilderness around Denali, at 20,310 feet the highest mountain in North America. A single 92-mile road winds into the park, and most visitors travel it by bus, scanning braided rivers and open tundra for grizzly bears, moose, caribou, Dall sheep and wolves. The mountain is often hidden in its own weather, which makes a clear view all the more memorable.
facts.best_time: Late May–mid-September, when buses run; late August brings autumn colours on the tundra.
facts.how_to_get_there: The park entrance is about 4 hours’ drive (or a scenic Alaska Railroad journey) north of Anchorage and about 2 hours south of Fairbanks.
facts.good_to_know: Private vehicles are limited to the first 15 miles of the park road. A landslide has closed the road beyond about Mile 43 in recent seasons—check NPS for current bus destinations.

facts.why_go: Joshua Tree protects the meeting point of the Mojave and Colorado deserts in southern California. The higher Mojave side is studded with spiky Joshua trees and piles of rounded granite boulders that draw climbers from around the world, while the lower Colorado Desert holds the Cholla Cactus Garden. Keys View looks over the Coachella Valley, and the park’s dark skies make for spectacular stargazing.

The Chain of Craters Road descends past lava flows to dramatic sea cliffs, and trails cross the floor of Kīlauea Iki crater and pass through the Nāhuku lava tube.

facts.one_liner: The deepest lake in the United States, intensely blue inside a collapsed volcano.
facts.why_go: Crater Lake fills the caldera left when Mount Mazama collapsed about 7,700 years ago. At 1,943 feet, it is the deepest lake in the United States, and fed almost entirely by rain and snow, its water is famously clear and deep blue. Rim Drive circles the caldera past viewpoints over Wizard Island, and in summer the Cleetwood Cove Trail leads down to the shore for boat tours.
facts.best_time: July–September, when Rim Drive and trails are usually snow-free.
facts.how_to_get_there: About 1.5 hours’ drive from Medford (MFR) or Klamath Falls; Rim Village is open year-round via the south entrance.
facts.good_to_know: The area gets some of the heaviest snowfall in the US—much of the park is closed for over half the year. Boat tours require tickets and a steep hike back up.

facts.best_time: June–September, when the lagoons are at their fullest.
facts.how_to_get_there: Fly to São Luís, then travel about 4 hours by road to Barreirinhas, the main gateway; tours continue by 4×4 or boat.
facts.good_to_know: Visits are by licensed tour. There is no shade on the dunes—bring water, a hat and sunscreen.

facts.one_liner: Beagle Channel shores and subantarctic forest at the end of the world.
facts.why_go: Tierra del Fuego National Park on the Beagle Channel is Argentina’s southernmost national park. Coastal trails wind through southern beech forest to bays dotted with islets, while Lago Roca, Ensenada Zaratiegui and Lapataia Bay—where Argentina’s National Route 3 ends—are classic stops. The Southern Fuegian Railway, the ‘End of the World Train’, also runs into the park.
facts.best_time: November–March, the southern summer, for the longest days and mildest weather.
facts.how_to_get_there: The park is about 12 km west of Ushuaia, which has flights from Buenos Aires.
facts.good_to_know: Weather is changeable even in summer—carry waterproof layers. A park entry fee applies.
